consensus_summary: All four blind responses converge on a core: righteousness is primarily right standing before God — a status of being in right relationship with Him, conformed to His character and standard — most prominently understood (in Protestant-dominated English teaching) as Christ's righteousness imputed/credited to the believer through faith apart from works (Gen 15:6; Rom 3:21-26; 4:3-8; Phil 3:9; 2 Cor 5:21). Ethical conduct, infused transformation, covenant faithfulness, and social justice are recognized as alternatives or secondary registers, but the primary identification is a conferred relational-forensic status.
book_summary: The book defines righteousness as 'Right-living': God is Right-Living by definition, and for those under His authority, righteousness is His commandments lived out (Deut 6:25; Ps 119:172; 1 John 3:7). Its opposite is Sin. The book explicitly flags the common teaching (imputed right standing received by faith, with right-living as subsequent fruit) as the view it departs from: for the book, lived obedience is not the fruit of righteousness but righteousness itself, with the imputation texts (Rom 4:4-8; Phil 3:9) handled through cross-referenced chapters on Paul's wage/debt/law vocabulary and on righteousness 'given and worn.'
consensus_core_identification: Righteousness = right standing before God: a status of right relationship and conformity to God's standard, paradigmatically conferred by God through faith (imputed/credited), not achieved by works; conduct is fruit or evidence of that status.
book_core_identification: Righteousness = right-living: the actual practice of God's commandments lived out under His authority; God Himself is righteous by definition of His right action, and a person is righteous by doing righteousness.
boundary_disagreement: Under the consensus, a person is righteous by virtue of a divinely conferred status received through faith, even while conduct remains imperfect; under the book, righteousness just is commandments lived out, so a believer with imputed status but without right-living would not, on the book's definition, be righteous, and one who 'doeth righteousness' is righteous (1 John 3:7). The book reclassifies status-holders and doers: the consensus's central case (declared-righteous believer, conduct as fruit) is redefined so that the conduct itself constitutes the righteousness.
material_contradiction: The consensus identifies righteousness primarily as a forensic/relational status distinct from, and prior to, right conduct ('right standing... rather than righteousness achieved by human works'). The book identifies righteousness as the conduct itself ('His commandments lived out'), and its common-view note explicitly marks the imputed-standing definition as the teaching it displaces. Both cannot be the primary identification of the same term in the same sense: status conferred apart from works versus works lived out are competing definitions, not nuances of one another.
rationale: The book's definition is not merely a narrowing of the consensus core; it replaces the central referent. The consensus core is a conferred right standing (with conduct as fruit); the book makes the conduct the definition and relegates the standing-view to a 'commonly taught' position it corrects. This meets the DIVERGENT test: accepting the book requires rejecting the consensus's primary identification. It is not NOVEL, because the book's view is recognizably close to listed alternatives (ethical uprightness, 1 John 3:7; the infused/transformative reading; OT tsedaqah as right conduct) — but those are alternatives to, not the consensus's, core, and the classification is against the consensus primary. Extensionally there is heavy overlap (many people count as righteous on both views), but the criteria for membership are reclassified, so PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION rather than disjoint referents.
strongest_objection: One could argue REFINED: the consensus itself concedes righteousness 'encompasses' conformity to God's standard and right conduct (Responses B, C, D each name moral uprightness within or alongside the primary meaning), so the book merely re-weights an admitted component rather than replacing the referent. Additionally, the book cites Rom 4:4-8 and Phil 3:9 and cross-references a chapter on righteousness 'given and worn,' suggesting it may retain a conferred dimension and thus preserve the consensus category. Against this, the book's own common-view note frames imputed right standing as the position being displaced, which signals a competing core identification rather than a boundary adjustment.
